criteria.name: visual_grounding
criteria.description: Visual grounding evaluates whether every factual claim in the answer strictly corresponds to what is visibly present in the image — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, colors, textures, structural support, and quantifiable features — without fabricating, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. It is evaluated only after confirming factual consistency with the image — and applies exclusively to factual, observable visual elements (not aesthetic, interpretive, or non-visual metadata). Annotators must verify each claim against the visual record using direct observation or conservative inference from unambiguous cues — not mental reconstruction, speculation, or external knowledge. Hallucinations — defined as fabricating non-existent visual elements, actions, relationships, or attributes — are always penalized, regardless of contextual plausibility. Misrepresentations — such as misidentifying visible elements (e.g., mistaking a ceiling light for a TV) — are penalized only if they misrepresent the visual record; misidentifications of color or texture (e.g., ‘red’ vs. ‘orange’) are not hallucinations if the element is visibly present. Omission of clearly visible elements is penalized only if the element is semantically essential to answering the question or if its omission contradicts the visual record — otherwise, omission is not a violation. Contextually supported inferences (e.g., inferring ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window or ‘on shelves’ from visible shelf structure) are acceptable and not penalized, as long as they are grounded in direct visual cues and do not fabricate non-existent elements. Descriptive phrases like ‘mixed together’ or ‘small portion’ are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual scene — even if not perfectly uniform — as long as they are grounded in the visual record. Visual grounding does not penalize accurate, conservative, or relative descriptions of size and position — even if they differ from more absolute claims — as long as they are visually supported. It does not penalize accurate descriptions of visible postures (e.g., ‘legs bent’) — even if non-standard — or emotional/behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’) — as long as they are visually grounded and contextually plausible. Aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘eye-catching’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — even if subjective — as long as it does not imply hallucinated visual attributes. Calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly a tent’, ‘appears to be’) is rewarded for ambiguous visual elements — not penalized — and must be used instead of omission. The criterion applies only to factual, observable visual elements — not to subjective, aesthetic, or interpretive judgments — which are evaluated under other criteria. It is evaluated only after confirming factual consistency — but only applies to factual, observable visual elements. Visual grounding does not penalize overestimation of counts (e.g., ‘at least twelve’) if the number is visually supported — only if the claim exceeds visible evidence. It does not require pixel-perfect spatial precision — only contextually accurate spatial relationships (e.g., ‘in front of’, ‘behind’, ‘scattered’) — and penalizes only when misrepresentations are visually evident. Composite surfaces (e.g., whiteboards, canvases) and attached items (e.g., sticky notes) must be counted as distinct visual elements. Common or colloquial terms (e.g., ‘water scooter’ for jet ski) are acceptable if they do not misrepresent the object’s core visual identity — and are not hallucinations. Structural context (e.g., walls, floors, rods, shelves) must be described accurately — even if not central to the question — as they are critical visual elements. Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record — and descriptive phrases matching labels are not hallucinations — they are rewarded. The criterion must not be conflated with factual consistency or specificity — grounding is about fidelity to visual presence, not accuracy of interpretation. When visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer must reflect the ambiguity, not invent or omit. The criterion is always evaluated after confirming factual consistency — but only applies to factual, observable visual elements. If an answer contains hallucinations or misrepresents visible elements, it is automatically disqualified from visual grounding evaluation — regardless of other criteria. Visual grounding does not penalize for plausible inferences, minor misidentifications, or stylized depictions — unless they misrepresent or omit clearly visible elements. The criterion is inapplicable to non-living, stylized, or artistic representations unless their visual form is being misrepresented — and does not penalize descriptions of their pose or structure if they are visually present. Visual grounding is not applicable to non-visual elements — such as titles, artist attribution, or stylistic labels — which are evaluated under factual_consistency_with_the_image. The goal is to reward answers that reflect all visually present elements with precision — even if minor or ambiguous — and penalize only hallucinations and omissions of critical visual elements — not contextually accurate or inferential descriptions that are visually grounded. Annotators must prioritize including all visible elements — not omitting them — unless they are semantically irrelevant. Hallucinations — including misrepresentations — are always penalized, regardless of plausibility or partial visual grounding. The criterion does not penalize accurate, visually grounded descriptions — even if they are not the most common or expected interpretation — and must avoid penalizing answers for being contextually accurate, visually grounded, or factually consistent. Descriptions of visual elements as compositional, abstract, or symbolic — such as ‘human-shaped’ or ‘stylized human silhouette’ — are acceptable — as long as they are visually grounded — and not penalized for being subjective or contextually grounded. Labeled text within the image must be reported accurately — not inferred or overruled by other visual cues — and misrepresentation of labeled elements (e.g., describing the cave as ‘wooden’ when labeled ‘gloomy cave’) is a violation, even if the label is stylized. Visual grounding does not penalize for describing visible elements as ‘in a line’ — as long as the visual arrangement is linear — and penalizes only when the arrangement is not visually linear. Descriptions of visible elements as ‘small portion’, ‘minor part’, or ‘near the edge’ are acceptable — even if not dominant — and ‘most of the space’, ‘largest object’, or ‘center’ are only valid if visually verifiable. The criterion must explicitly state that all hallucinations — including misrepresentations and fabrications — are equally penalized, regardless of contextual plausibility or partial visual grounding. Visual grounding requires strict correspondence to visible elements, not contextual reinterpretation. It must explicitly warn against using ‘contextually plausible’ as a justification for hallucinations or misrepresentations — and must prioritize complete visual fidelity over partial or inferential claims. The criterion must explicitly separate visual grounding from factual consistency — visual grounding evaluates visual elements only — not real-world facts — and must not penalize answers for factual errors like misidentifying a landmark. It must also clarify that visual hallucinations (fabricating non-existent visual elements) are the only grounds for disqualification — not factual errors. The criterion must explicitly state that visual grounding is evaluated independently of other criteria — and that workers must evaluate visual grounding even when factual consistency is violated — as long as the visual description is grounded in the image. The criterion must explicitly warn workers not to confuse factual errors with visual hallucinations — and to evaluate visual grounding based on visual evidence alone. The criterion must explicitly define 'hallucination' as fabricating non-existent visual elements — not misidentifying or misrepresenting visible ones — and must penalize only those. It must also clarify that accurate descriptions of visible elements (even if contextually surprising) are rewarded — not penalized — as long as they are visually supported. The criterion must explicitly state that visual grounding rewards fidelity to the visual record — not penalizing accurate, grounded descriptions — and must warn against conflating misrepresentation with hallucination. The criterion must explicitly state that visual grounding is not applicable to non-literal, metaphorical, or symbolic descriptions — unless those descriptions are grounded in observable visual cues — to avoid misapplication to stylized or artistic representations. The criterion must explicitly state that visual grounding is not a ‘less is more’ heuristic — and that omitting visible elements is penalized only if semantically essential — not for being vague or non-essential. The criterion must explicitly clarify that relative spatial descriptions like 'small portion', 'minor part', or 'near the edge' are acceptable if visually accurate — even if not dominant — and that absolute claims like 'most of the space', 'largest object', or 'center' are only valid if visually verifiable. The criterion must explicitly prohibit penalizing 'small portion' for being non-absolute — and require visual evidence for claims like 'most' or 'largest'. The criterion must explicitly clarify that 'position near the edge' is not a hallucination if the object is visibly located at the boundary — and that 'central' is only accurate if visually supported — not if it is inferable from context or proportion. The criterion must explicitly state that 'taking up a small portion' is not a hallucination — even if the object appears large — as long as the description reflects the visual record — and penalize only when the description exceeds visual evidence. The criterion must explicitly state that visual grounding requires including all visible elements — not just avoiding hallucinations — and must clarify that omission of visible elements (unless semantically irrelevant) is a violation. It should also explicitly warn against conflating omission of non-critical elements with visual grounding, and instruct workers to prioritize including visible elements over omitting them. The criterion must explicitly state that hallucinations are always penalized — regardless of plausibility — and that omission of non-essential elements is not a violation — but that workers must not omit visible elements unless they are semantically irrelevant. The criterion should include explicit examples to guide workers on when to omit vs. when to include — particularly in ambiguous or stylized images. The criterion must explicitly clarify that overestimation (e.g., 'at least five', 'up to ten') is not penalized if visually supported — and that 'at least' or 'possibly' or 'up to' are acceptable if grounded — to prevent workers from conflating 'visual grounding' with 'accuracy' or 'minimalism'. It should also explicitly state that visual grounding does not penalize contextually grounded inferences — even if they are not exact — and that 'five' is not a hallucination if it is visually supported. The criterion must be rewritten to explicitly prohibit penalizing overestimation when visually supported — and to explicitly state that visual grounding does not require absolute precision — only fidelity to what is visually present. It should also explicitly warn against penalizing 'overestimation' — even if it exceeds the worker’s perception — as long as it is visually supported — and should explicitly state that 'at least' or 'up to' are acceptable if grounded — to prevent misapplication. The criterion must also explicitly clarify that visual grounding does not penalize contextually grounded inferences — even if they are not exact — and that 'five' is not a hallucination if it is visually supported — to prevent workers from misapplying the criterion to non-hallucinated claims. Finally, it should explicitly state that visual grounding does not penalize 'overestimation' — even if it exceeds the worker’s perception — as long as it is visually supported — and should explicitly warn against penalizing 'overestimation' — even if it exceeds the worker’s perception — as long as it is visually supported — to prevent misapplication. The criterion must explicitly require first verifying object identity (e.g., the bird is a sparrow, not a Velociraptor) before any inference — and must penalize any claim that misidentifies or fabricates visual elements, even if biologically plausible. It should clarify that 'contextually supported inference' only applies to visible elements (e.g., 'on a chair') — not to non-visible biological or evolutionary claims. The criterion must also explicitly state that it does not evaluate biological plausibility — only visual fidelity — and must not be used to penalize accurate, visually grounded inferences about behavior or ecology if they are not hallucinations. Finally, it should explicitly warn against applying visual grounding to non-visual or speculative biological claims — and must require verification of object identity before any inference. The criterion must explicitly define 'hallucination' as any claim that contradicts the visual record — not as any added detail — and must penalize only when the visual evidence is absent or ambiguous. It must clarify that 'visual presence' includes clearly observable features like posture, facial expressions, and background colors — and must explicitly state that subjective interpretations (e.g., 'dark brown background') are acceptable if they match the visual record. It must also clarify that emotional or behavioral inferences (e.g., 'smiling') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported — and must reward accurate descriptions of visible elements, even if not explicitly labeled. Finally, it must explicitly warn against penalizing plausible, visible details — and must emphasize that 'visual grounding' is about fidelity to the visual record — not about avoiding any added detail — as long as it is factually accurate and visually supported. The criterion must explicitly state that descriptions like 'human-shaped' or 'stylized human silhouette' are acceptable — as long as they are visually grounded — and not penalized for being subjective or contextually grounded. It should clarify that 'human-shaped' is a valid description of a visible silhouette — even if it is stylized — and that it is not a hallucination. The criterion should also explicitly warn against penalizing accurate, visually grounded descriptions for being 'subjective' or 'contextual' — even if they are not perfectly literal. Finally, the criterion should explicitly state that 'human-shaped' or similar descriptions are not hallucinations — even if they are not literal — as long as they are visually supported and do not misrepresent the visual record. The criterion must explicitly allow descriptions of visual elements as compositional, abstract, or symbolic — as long as they are grounded in the visual record — and must not penalize for describing elements that are visually present, even if they resemble actions. It must also clarify that 'hallucination' refers only to fabricating non-existent visual elements — not misrepresenting compositional or symbolic elements — to avoid penalizing accurate, stylized descriptions. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that visual grounding does not penalize for describing compositional or symbolic elements — even if they resemble actions — as long as they are visually present — to avoid penalizing accurate, stylized descriptions. The criterion must explicitly distinguish between hallucinations (fabricating non-existent elements) and misidentifications (mislabeling existing elements) — and must clarify that misidentifications of state (e.g., 'cold needles') are allowed if the element is visibly present — while hallucinations (e.g., 'cold ice') are always penalized. It must also explicitly state that descriptive aesthetic terms (e.g., 'messy') are not hallucinations — and must not penalize them. Furthermore, it must explicitly clarify that misrepresentations of arrangement (e.g., 'in a line') are hallucinations only if the arrangement is not visually linear — and must penalize such misrepresentations. The criterion must also be revised to explicitly state that 'cold ice' is a hallucination — fabricating a substance — while 'cold needles' is a misidentification of state — which is allowed if the element is visibly present. The agent must be instructed to treat 'messy' as a non-hallucinated descriptive aesthetic term — and to distinguish between hallucinations (fabricating non-existent elements) and misidentifications (mislabeling existing elements). The criterion must also be revised to explicitly state that 'in a line' is a hallucination if the arrangement is not visually linear — which it is not — and to penalize such misrepresentations. The criterion must explicitly state that omitting visible elements is not a hallucination — and that 'not visible' or 'not clearly visible' is a factually grounded, acceptable description — not a misrepresentation. It must also clarify that 'misrepresentation' applies only to false claims — not to honest descriptions of absence or ambiguity — and that visual_grounding rewards accuracy in describing what is visible — not what is absent. Furthermore, the criterion should explicitly reward honest descriptions of ambiguity — and must clarify that visual evidence must be confirmed — not assumed — and that any claim that contradicts the visual record (even if plausible) is a hallucination — not a misrepresentation. Finally, the criterion must explicitly warn against penalizing accurate descriptions of absence or ambiguity — and must state that 'not visible' or 'not clearly visible' is always acceptable — even if the element is semantically relevant — and that 'misrepresentation' only applies to false claims — not to honest, visually supported omissions or ambiguities. The criterion should explicitly permit contextually grounded behavioral or social inferences (e.g., 'waiting for their turn') as long as they are plausible within the visual context and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements. It should also clarify that such inferences are not hallucinations if they are supported by the scene’s implied context (e.g., group activity, shared space) and do not contradict visible structure or actions. The current description is too restrictive by penalizing any speculative inference — even if contextually plausible — which leads to misalignment with human preference. The criterion should distinguish between hallucinations (fabricating non-existent visual elements) and contextually grounded inferences (interpreting behavior or social context without fabricating visual evidence). The criterion must explicitly define 'hallucination' as fabricating non-existent visual elements — not misidentifying or misrepresenting visible ones — and must penalize only those. It must also clarify that accurate descriptions of visible elements (even if contextually surprising) are rewarded — not penalized — as long as they are visually supported. The description should emphasize that visual grounding rewards fidelity to the visual record — not penalizing accurate, grounded descriptions — and must warn against conflating misrepresentation with hallucination. Additionally, it should explicitly state that the criterion does not penalize accurate descriptions of visible elements — even if they are not the most common or expected interpretation — and must avoid penalizing answers for being contextually accurate, visually grounded, or factually consistent. The criterion should also clarify that 'misrepresentation' is only penalized if it misrepresents the visual record — not if it correctly describes a visible element — and must be explicitly contrasted with 'hallucination'.

criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with the visually verifiable elements present in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless they are explicitly irrelevant to the question’s literal intent. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record.

criteria.name: completeness
criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or direct visual contradictions is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation, regardless of detail level. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all visually present elements that are semantically required to fully answer the question’s literal intent — defined as elements directly necessary to satisfy the question’s core factual demand (e.g., object identity, spatial relationships, posture, motion, or contextually grounded actions). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, completeness is inapplicable. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all semantically essential visual components — not all visible details, nor aesthetic descriptors, nor speculative inferences — and omission of clearly visible, semantically essential elements (e.g., posture when asked ‘what is the person doing?’) is penalized. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or contextually unsupported details (e.g., ‘a camel’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) unless they are visually grounded and semantically relevant to answering the question — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question’s literal intent. If two answers are factually consistent, the one that includes more semantically essential, visually present elements wins — but only if those elements are not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to override factual consistency — factual consistency is the non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions. Examples: For ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘standing’ is essential; ‘wearing a red shirt’ is non-essential unless the question asks about clothing. For ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a visible object is incomplete; for ‘What is the object?’, omitting visible shape or color is incomplete if those are essential to identification. Completeness does not reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., color misidentification) if the core object or action is correctly described and visually grounded. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — but it should not be used to penalize minor factual errors that do not undermine the overall factual consistency or visual grounding. Finally, completeness does not apply to questions where the context is not visually relevant (e.g., team identification, jersey norms) unless explicitly required by the question’s intent. The criterion must explicitly define 'semantically essential' as elements required by the question’s literal intent — not architectural or structural features — and must clarify that contextual, non-essential details (like a Coca-Cola box) are still 'complete' if visually present, and that omitting such elements does not constitute incompleteness unless they are directly relevant to answering the question. It must also explicitly exclude architectural elements from being considered 'essential' unless the question is about room structure or layout. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only evaluated for factually consistent answers — and that if both candidates are factually inconsistent, neither is eligible for completeness evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). It must also clarify that a factual error (like misidentifying color) disqualifies an answer from completeness evaluation, regardless of how well it describes other visible elements. Additionally, the criterion should specify that if one answer is factually consistent and the other is not, the consistent one should be preferred — but if both are factually inconsistent, completeness is not applicable and the worker must rely on other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only applicable when the question’s literal intent requires specific visual elements beyond simple count or identification — e.g., spatial arrangement, functional use, or configuration — and must not penalize omissions of non-essential details (like spatial distribution) when the core factual requirement (e.g., count) is satisfied. It must also explicitly state that 'semantically essential' elements are defined only within the context of factually correct answers — and that any claim that is factually wrong (even if more specific) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. The criterion must explicitly prohibit rewarding speculative or contextually inferred arrangements that are not visually supported — even if they seem ‘semantically essential’. It must clarify that completeness only applies to literal, factual descriptions — not interpretive or inferred structures — and must penalize any answer that misrepresents the visual arrangement, even if it seems plausible. The criterion should also specify that ‘semantically essential’ elements must be visually present or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues — not speculative reconstruction — and must not reward hallucinated structures even if they seem ‘logical’ or ‘contextually appropriate’. Finally, it should clarify that completeness does not apply to questions asking for ‘how’ or ‘why’ — which might imply interpretation — and must be strictly applied to literal, factual descriptions. The criterion must explicitly state that 'semantically required' elements are defined by the question’s literal intent, not by contextual or interpretive assumptions. It must also clarify that adding non-essential, visually present details is not a strength under completeness — and that factual consistency is a non-negotiable prerequisite. Furthermore, the criterion should warn annotators that 'semantically required' does not mean 'contextually relevant' or 'socially appropriate' — and that visual presence alone is insufficient if the element is not required by the question. Finally, the criterion must explicitly forbid using completeness to override factual consistency — and must clarify that if one answer is hallucinated, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of detail level. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness rewards inclusion of all visually present, semantically essential elements — not omitting them for stylistic or aesthetic reasons. It must clarify that 'essential' means necessary for answering the question's literal intent — not minimal or concise. The description should penalize omission of visually present elements unless they are irrelevant to the question — and must explicitly forbid penalizing accurate, visually grounded details for being 'non-essential' or 'non-critical' unless they are genuinely irrelevant. The criterion should also clarify that 'completeness' is not about conciseness or accuracy of terminology — only about covering the visually necessary elements. Finally, it should explicitly warn against penalizing answers for including visually present, semantically relevant details that are not required for literal accuracy — even if they are not the most 'precise' or 'concise'.

criteria.name: specificity
criteria.description: Specificity evaluates the granularity and precision of visually verifiable details in an answer — including object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, brand names, labels, or contextual elements — but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding: if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation entirely, and no comparison should be made under this criterion. Specificity rewards answers that add accurate, non-hallucinated, granular details — even minor or non-essential ones — as long as they are visually verifiable and do not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. It does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral or environmental inferences (e.g., ‘waiting for their turn’ from posture, ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported and not hallucinated. However, it DOES penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘visually appealing’, ‘mirror effect’) that lacks visual grounding — as these are subjective and not descriptive of visual elements. Specificity does not reward speculative inferences — but does reward inclusion of verifiable, granular details like ‘a browser window’ — even if the action (e.g., ‘browsing’) is inferred. Hallucinations (fabricated objects, actions, or attributes not visible) are always penalized — even if highly detailed — and disqualify the answer from specificity evaluation. Specificity is not a tiebreaker — it applies only to factually consistent and visually grounded answers, and preference must be determined using foundational criteria (visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image) first. It is not about linguistic creativity or detail quantity — it is about precision in describing what is visually present and factually correct. Annotators should prioritize accurate, granular descriptions over vague or generic ones — but only if they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity must not override or compensate for violations of visual grounding or factual consistency — granularity is irrelevant if the answer is hallucinated or misrepresents the visual record. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative detail — and specificity is not applicable. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ is more specific than ‘a red sedan parked’ — both are grounded and factually consistent. ‘A cat with a golden collar’ is penalized — it is a hallucination. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ is rewarded — if the child is visually present. ‘A person with an angry expression’ is penalized — if ‘angry’ is not visually verifiable. ‘A person with a red jacket’ is rewarded — if the jacket is visible. ‘A person with a red jacket that is eye-catching’ is penalized — ‘eye-catching’ is aesthetic and not visually verifiable. ‘A person browsing a web page’ is not penalized — if a browser window is visible — but ‘a person browsing a web page on a laptop’ is rewarded — if the laptop is visible. ‘A person waiting for their turn’ is penalized — if not visually implied — even if plausible. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt’ is rewarded — if the logo is visible — even if not central. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt that says ‘Nike’’ is rewarded — if the text is visible — even if not central. Specificity must not be used to evaluate or override factual consistency — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer. It is only applicable for factual, visually grounded answers — and does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or non-visual judgments — unless grounded in observable visual cues. The goal is to reward answers that add precision and granularity to the description of visually present elements — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresenting the visual record. Annotators should prioritize verifiable, granular details — even if minor or non-essential — over vague or generic descriptions — as long as they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity is evaluated only after factual consistency and visual grounding are confirmed — and is never applied to hallucinated or factually inconsistent answers. Additionally, specificity does not apply to artistic, abstract, or stylized visual elements — such as ‘pattern design’, ‘arc’, or ‘composition’ — unless they are visually verifiable or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues. Descriptive aesthetic terms (e.g., ‘eye-catching’) are only allowed if they are visually grounded — and must not be penalized for being non-essential. Contextually grounded inferences are rewarded if visually supported — even if not explicitly visible — as long as they are plausible and not hallucinated. Specificity is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded answers — and such answers must be disqualified from the entire preference comparison before any criterion evaluation. Finally, specificity rewards the most accurate, visually verifiable description — not the most semantically labeled one — and penalizes any answer that uses a semantic label (e.g., ‘logo’) that is not visually verifiable — while rewarding the answer that provides the most precise visual description — even if it uses descriptive terms (e.g., ‘human-shaped pattern’).

criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
criteria.description: The answer should reflect confidence appropriately. If the image is ambiguous, the answer should indicate uncertainty (e.g., “possibly” or “likely”) without overstating certainty. Annotators penalize overconfidence in uncertain situations and reward humility when appropriate.

criteria.name: logical_consistency
criteria.description: The answer must be internally coherent and free from contradictions. For example, if it says an animal is both “calm” and “in pain,” or that objects are “on opposite sides” while also “centered,” it lacks logical consistency. Annotators evaluate whether the answer’s internal logic aligns with the visual evidence.

criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates the reasonableness of behavioral, emotional, or contextual inferences about living beings (humans, animals, or plants) — such as ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’, ‘leaning forward’, ‘waiting’, or ‘content’ — based solely on direct, unambiguous visual cues (e.g., facial expression, posture, gaze, motion blur, physical contact). It is ONLY applicable when the answer is already factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — and must be applied strictly as a tiebreaker between two factually consistent and visually grounded answers. If either visual grounding or factual consistency is violated, the answer is disqualified from plausibility evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image). Plausibility does not apply to non-living subjects (e.g., logos, statues, abstract art, inanimate objects) — and workers must report ‘inapplicable’ when the subject is non-living. It also does not apply to spatial or structural claims (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’, ‘on a shelf’) — which are evaluated under visual_grounding — nor to material, functional, or design claims (e.g., ‘made of metal’, ‘has a logo’, ‘on a laptop’) — which are evaluated under factual_consistency_with_the_image. Plausibility is NOT a disqualification tool — and must never be used to override visual grounding, factual consistency, or to resolve ties involving factually incorrect answers. It does not penalize subjective or contextually reasonable inferences (e.g., ‘serious’, ‘playful’, ‘arrogant’) — as long as they are visually grounded — and must not be used to penalize plausible, posture-based inferences even if they seem contextually ‘off’ — e.g., ‘leaning forward’ is acceptable if posture supports it, even if the context seems odd. It does not evaluate descriptive style, completeness, specificity, or accuracy of terminology — only whether the inferred behavior or context is biologically or physically reasonable given the visual evidence — and must never be used to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative inference — and plausibility is not applicable. The goal is to reward accurate, visually grounded inferences that are contextually reasonable — and penalize only falsehoods or hallucinations — not subjective interpretations or minimalism. Annotators must reject any inference that contradicts the visual record — even if it seems ‘reasonable’ — and must avoid using plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. This criterion is strictly for behavioral or contextual inferences — not literal visual descriptions (e.g., ‘man holding woman’s hand’) — which are factually consistent if visually supported — and not for spatial or structural claims — which are evaluated under visual_grounding. Plausibility does not override visual grounding — and if a spatial claim is visually supported, it is not a hallucination — even if contextually ambiguous. The criterion must not be applied to non-living subjects — and must explicitly warn workers not to apply it to non-living subjects — even if they describe behavior or context — and must require workers to report ‘inapplicable’ when the subject is non-living. It must also explicitly state that it is not a preference rule — and must never be used to resolve ties involving factually incorrect answers — which must be disqualified under other criteria. Plausibility is not applicable to questions asking for factual or structural claims — and workers must defer to visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image for such claims. Finally, the criterion must explicitly clarify that it is not a filter for environmental context — and that environmental claims should be evaluated under other criteria — to prevent misapplication.

criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
criteria.description: Multimodal_coherence evaluates whether an answer’s internal claims — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, postures, and inferred states — are logically consistent with each other, but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. If either factual consistency or visual grounding is violated, the answer is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and preference must be determined by other foundational criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image). This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker and does NOT penalize hallucinations or misidentifications — those are handled by foundational criteria. It rewards answers that avoid internal contradictions (e.g., describing an object as ‘on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path) — but does NOT penalize plausible, contextually grounded inferences that are visually supported — even if not explicitly visible. It also does NOT penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) as long as it does not imply hallucinated visual attributes. It evaluates only visual fidelity and internal consistency — not linguistic style, completeness, plausibility, or specificity. Annotators must: (1) first confirm factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from all criteria — and multimodal_coherence is inapplicable; (2) check for contradictions between claims (e.g., posture vs. action); (3) verify that inferences are grounded in observable cues (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ from posture, not ‘browsing Apple web pages’ unless Apple logos are visible); (4) penalize only when a claim misrepresents the visual record — not when it is speculative or contextually reasonable. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer internal contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred — but only after confirming factual consistency. Spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are not hallucinations if visually implied by perspective or depth — and posture-based inferences (e.g., ‘wiping hair from head’) are rewarded as conservative, visually supported inferences — not penalized as speculation. Emotional or behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’) are not hallucinations if visually supported — and should not be penalized for being subjective or interpretive. Aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — as long as it does not imply hallucinations. The criterion applies ONLY to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and any answer with factual errors is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation, regardless of internal consistency. It is NOT applicable to static, non-motion-related questions — and should not be used to override visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image. When visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should use calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly a tent’) — not speculative reconstruction — and multimodal_coherence should not penalize this. The goal is to reward answers that are faithful to the visual record — not stylistically conservative, vague, or overly specific — and to penalize only hallucinations or contradictions — not plausible, contextually grounded inferences. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must never apply multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or make conservative inferences. The criterion must explicitly state: (a) ‘conservative inference’ applies only to ambiguous visual cues — not to clear, observable behaviors — and must not penalize accurate emotional or behavioral descriptions when they are visually grounded; (b) ‘unsupported speculation’ applies only to claims that misrepresent the image’s structure or content — not to accurate but non-essential details or plausible, contextually grounded inferences; (c) ‘visual misrepresentation’ applies only to claims that contradict verifiable visual evidence — not to plausible, contextually grounded inferences or spatial relationships inferred from perspective; (d) ‘factually consistent’ means claims are supported by the image’s visual record — not that they are ‘visually identical’ or ‘perfectly accurate’ — and misidentifications (e.g., calling a cake ‘cupcakes’) are not automatically grounds for disqualification — only if they contradict the visual record; (e) ‘factually consistent’ is evaluated against the image — not against an external standard — and should not be used to penalize accurate but less specific descriptions; (f) multimodal_coherence does not evaluate or penalize terminology precision, linguistic style, or specificity — only hallucinations and contradictions — and should not be used to resolve ties based on terminology accuracy — preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity); (g) spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are not hallucinations if they are visually implied by perspective or depth — even if not explicitly labeled — and ‘conservative inference’ does not apply to clearly implied spatial relationships — and must not penalize spatial claims that are logically implied by the image’s structure — even if not perfectly explicit. The criterion must also explicitly: (h) reward contextually grounded inferences — including flavor, texture, or composition — when visually supported — even if not explicitly labeled; (i) clarify that ‘flatly placed’ is not a misrepresentation if it accurately describes spatial arrangement; (j) remove or clarify the penalization of ‘unsupported speculation’ to avoid penalizing plausible, visually grounded inferences — and must explicitly define ‘unsupported speculation’ as fabricating non-existent visual attributes (e.g., ‘matcha flavored’ if no visual cue exists) — not as reasonable interpretation of color or texture; (k) emphasize that spatial descriptions (like ‘flatly placed’) are not hallucinations unless they contradict the visual record — and must explicitly warn against penalizing accurate, non-hallucinated descriptions of position or orientation; (l) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not applicable to factually inconsistent answers — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) when foundational criteria are violated — to avoid misapplication in cases where one answer is disqualified; (m) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and emphasize that it is only for evaluating internal consistency among factually consistent answers; (n) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, specificity, completeness) — not by multimodal_coherence — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence should not be applied to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or internally coherent; (o) explicitly distinguish between ‘visual misrepresentation’ (contradicting verifiable visual evidence) and ‘contextually misleading’ or ‘structurally surprising’ descriptions — and must not penalize accurate descriptions of static, structural features — even if they are not ‘normal’ or ‘standard’; (p) explicitly define ‘internal contradiction’ as a misrepresentation of visual evidence — not as any inference that contradicts a definitive visual cue — and must clarify that cautious, contextually grounded inferences are not penalized — even if they contradict a definitive visual cue — as long as they are grounded in the visual record; (q) explicitly allow and reward contextually grounded inferences that are visually plausible — even if not explicitly visible — as long as they do not contradict the visual record; (r) explicitly state that negative claims (e.g., ‘no one is wearing jerseys’) are not penalized under ‘internal contradiction’ — as long as they are visually supported and contextually plausible; (s) explicitly reward conservative, depth-based spatial inferences like ‘behind’ — which are visually supported — and must explicitly penalize claims like ‘in front of’ — which are hallucinated spatial relationships — unless clearly depicted; (t) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is only applicable to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and that if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation — not penalized or evaluated under this criterion; (u) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and clarify that any candidate with factual errors is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and that the worker should defer to other criteria for comparison; (v) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) if the candidates are factually consistent and visually grounded — and that the criterion should not be used to penalize factual errors or misidentifications; (w) explicitly distinguish between literal physical motion (which requires visual evidence like motion blur or posture) and compositional or stylistic implications (which are acceptable if visually supported) — and must clarify that descriptions of implied action — such as ‘drawing an arc’ — are not hallucinations if they are consistent with the visual composition and do not contradict the scene’s structure; (x) explicitly state that ‘drawing an arc’ or ‘implied motion’ is allowed as long as it is grounded in visual composition — and must not penalize such descriptions as hallucinations unless they contradict the visual record; (y) explicitly prohibit using factual consistency to override visual grounding — and clarify that compositional interpretations are not hallucinations if they are contextually grounded and visually supported; (z) include guidance to treat stylistic or symbolic representations (e.g., ‘drawing an arc’) as non-hallucinated if they are consistent with the visual composition — and must not penalize them as factual inconsistencies. Additionally, the criterion must explicitly: (aa) state that aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — even if it appears to contradict a spatial description — as long as it is visually grounded and does not misrepresent the visual record; (ab) clarify that multimodal_coherence does not penalize internal contradictions between aesthetic and spatial descriptors — and should instead reward descriptive accuracy and visual fidelity; (ac) include examples of coexisting descriptors (e.g., ‘arranged in a line’ + ‘messy’) to prevent misapplication; (ad) explicitly state that the criterion does not penalize accurate, contextually grounded aesthetic descriptions — even if they seem to contradict spatial claims — and must be applied only after verifying factual consistency and visual grounding — not to override or penalize aesthetic interpretations. Finally, the criterion must explicitly: (ae) state that multimodal_coherence is not a substitute for factual_consistency_with_the_image — and that workers must first verify factual consistency before applying this criterion — and (af) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and clarify that any candidate with factual errors is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and that the worker should defer to other criteria for comparison. The criterion must also explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) — not by multimodal_coherence — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence is only a tool for evaluating internal consistency — not for resolving preference. The criterion must also clarify that when multiple factually consistent answers exist, preference must be determined by other criteria — not by multimodal_coherence — and that multimodal_coherence should not be applied to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or internally coherent. The criterion must also explicitly state that it does not evaluate or compare factually consistent answers — and that preference must be determined by other criteria — such as visual_grounding, specificity, or completeness — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence is only a tool for evaluating internal consistency — not for resolving preference. The criterion must also explicitly state that it is not applicable to factually inconsistent answers — and that preference must be determined by other criteria — not by defaulting to the factually consistent answer. It must also clarify that multimodal_coherence is only for evaluating internal consistency among factually consistent answers — and that it should not be used to override or substitute for foundational criteria. Additionally, it must explicitly warn against misapplying the criterion to factually inconsistent answers — and must clarify that preference must be determined by other criteria — not by defaulting to the factually consistent answer. Finally, it must explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference must be determined by other criteria — not by multimodal_coherence — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence should not be applied to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or internally coherent.

criteria.name: temporal_or_action_coherence
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer correctly describes motion, sequence, or timing that is either visually evident or strongly implied by the image — and only applies when the question explicitly involves dynamic elements (e.g., 'What is happening?', 'Is this person moving?', 'What sequence occurred?'). It does NOT apply to static object descriptions, spatial relationships, or non-temporal questions. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding; if an answer is factually incorrect or visually unsupported, this criterion is inapplicable and should not be used to penalize or reward. Only when the image contains motion cues (e.g., blur, mid-air posture, motion trails), implied sequence (e.g., objects arranged in temporal order), or time-sensitive context (e.g., a clock, action in progress) can this criterion be applied. It penalizes hallucinated or unsupported dynamic claims — e.g., describing a static person as 'jumping' without motion cues — but does NOT penalize plausible inferences grounded in visual state (e.g., 'a browser window implies browsing'). The criterion is inapplicable to abstract art, static compositions, or when the question is purely about object identification or presence/absence. Workers should avoid inferring motion from posture alone or aesthetic terms (e.g., 'dynamic' or 'gestural') unless explicitly supported by visual motion cues. When in doubt, the answer with stronger visual grounding and factual consistency should win — temporal coherence is never a tiebreaker if answers are equally grounded.

criteria.name: clarity_of_implied_relationships
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer explicitly or implicitly links visual elements in a way that is unambiguous and logically supported by the image — especially when describing spatial, causal, or functional relationships between objects. For example, if the image shows a person holding a cup, the answer should not ambiguously say 'the person has something in their hand' without specifying the object. Annotators should assess whether implied relationships (e.g., 'the cat is chasing the ball', 'the door is open because the handle is pulled') are grounded in visible evidence and avoid over-speculation. This criterion does not evaluate factual correctness or visual grounding directly — only how clearly relationships are communicated. It is applicable when the question asks about interactions, configurations, or dependencies — e.g., 'What is the relationship between the dog and the ball?', 'Why is the door open?'. If the relationship is visually ambiguous, the answer may use calibrated uncertainty — but if it invents or misrepresents relationships, it fails this criterion.

criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_ambiguous_scenes
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer appropriately uses calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly', 'appears to be', 'not clearly visible') ONLY when the visual evidence is objectively ambiguous — defined as cases where the image is blurred, occluded, low-resolution, or insufficient to support definitive claims about object identity, spatial relationships, or visual attributes — and ONLY after the answer has been confirmed as factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Uncertainty is NOT applied to clearly visible, non-ambiguous elements — which should be described confidently — nor to hallucinated, misidentified, or factually incorrect answers (which are disqualified under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image). Uncertainty is rewarded only when the visual record genuinely lacks clarity (e.g., partially obscured objects, indistinct textures, unresolvable spatial relationships) — not for contextually open interpretations, subjective emotional inferences (e.g., 'smiling', 'curious'), or non-literal descriptions (e.g., 'messy', 'intriguing') that are visually supported. It is NOT a tiebreaker — preference is determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, specificity, factual consistency) when answers are factually consistent and visually grounded. Uncertainty must NEVER be used to mask factual errors, misrepresentations, or omissions — and must never be applied to clearly visible elements, even if non-central or contextually open. The criterion is a refinement for factually correct answers — rewarding cautious language in ambiguous visual contexts — while prioritizing visual fidelity and factual accuracy over vague or overcautious interpretations. It does NOT penalize accurate, specific descriptions of clearly visible elements — even if non-essential — nor does it penalize contextually grounded inferences (e.g., 'browsing' from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported. The goal is to reward appropriate, contextually grounded caution in ambiguous scenes — not to enforce unnecessary vagueness or penalize confident descriptions in unambiguous ones. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must never use this criterion to override or justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. This criterion applies ONLY after factual consistency and visual grounding are confirmed — and is inapplicable to factually incorrect or visually ungrounded answers — which must be disqualified under other criteria first. Visual ambiguity is defined by visual clarity — not factual correctness — and factual errors are handled under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. The criterion is not a substitute for those criteria — and must not be used to evaluate or compare factually incorrect answers. It is only applicable to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and must be applied strictly to objectively ambiguous visual evidence — not to subjective interpretations, aesthetic judgments, or stylistic choices — even if visually supported. The criterion must explicitly state that uncertainty is not applicable to clearly visible elements — even if they are non-essential or contextually open — and that it does not penalize accurate, specific descriptions of clearly visible elements — even if non-essential. It must also explicitly prohibit penalizing contextually grounded inferences that are visually supported — even if they are not explicitly visible — as long as they are plausible and not hallucinated. Finally, the criterion must explicitly warn that uncertainty is not a tool for resolving factual errors or misidentifications — and must be applied only to visually ambiguous scenes — not to factually incorrect or hallucinated claims. Workers must explicitly report ‘inapplicable’ when all visual elements are clearly visible and unambiguous — to prevent misapplication. Uncertainty is not penalized for being ‘too cautious’ or ‘too vague’ — only for being misapplied to clearly visible elements or used to mask factual errors. Descriptions like ‘human-shaped pattern’ or ‘stylized human silhouette’ are allowed — as long as they are visually accurate — and are not penalized under this criterion. Subjective emotional or aesthetic language (e.g., ‘balanced’, ‘messy’) is permitted — as long as it is visually supported — and is not penalized as hallucination. Uncertainty is only applicable to visual ambiguity — not to contextually open inferences or biological speculation — and should not be applied to cases where the visual evidence is clear. This criterion does not evaluate or penalize factual accuracy — only the appropriateness of uncertainty language in ambiguous visual contexts — and must not be used to justify or mask misrepresentations — even if they are contextually plausible or visually supported. It is not a tool for resolving factual errors — and must not be used to compare factually incorrect answers — even if one is more cautious or specific. The criterion must be applied only to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and workers must disqualify such answers under other criteria before applying this one. It is not a tiebreaker — and preference must be determined by other criteria when answers are factually consistent and visually grounded. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that it does not penalize accurate, factually consistent, and visually grounded answers — even if they are more specific or descriptive — and that uncertainty is only for visual ambiguity — not for factual errors or misrepresentations.

criteria.name: visual_stability_and_motion_consistency
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s description of physical motion or stability (e.g., ‘running’, ‘leaning’, ‘stationary’, ‘in motion’, ‘in a state of rest’) is consistent with visually evident cues — such as motion blur, posture, dynamic framing, or static positioning — but ONLY when the question explicitly or implicitly involves motion, action, or physical stability (e.g., ‘What is happening?’, ‘Is this person moving?’, ‘Describe the action’, ‘What is the object doing?’). It is inapplicable to static, non-motion-related questions (e.g., object identification, spatial arrangement, background description, aesthetic judgments, or compositional analysis) — and must never be used to override or substitute for visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image. When applicable, it penalizes only definitive, factual claims that contradict visual evidence (e.g., describing a person as ‘running’ when no motion blur or dynamic posture is visible) — but does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘attending to her hair’) that do not imply actual motion or physical instability — as long as they are visually supported by posture or context. It does NOT penalize factual errors in object identity, color, or structure — those are handled under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. It also does NOT penalize stylistic, compositional, or contextual descriptors (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘unstructured’, ‘warehouse’) unless they imply motion or physical instability — and must not be conflated with physical motion or stability. The criterion is evaluated ONLY after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from evaluation under this criterion. It is not a tiebreaker — and if the question is static or non-motion-related, the criterion is inapplicable and workers must report ‘inapplicable’ and defer to other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image, semantic_alignment_with_question_intent) for static scenes. The criterion is strictly for motion/stability claims — not posture, seating, facial expressions, emotional states, or behavioral inferences — which are evaluated under other criteria. Visual evidence must be directly confirmed (e.g., motion blur, posture, spatial arrangement) — and descriptions must not infer motion or instability from ambiguous or non-visual cues (e.g., ‘no stop sign’ or ‘open space’). Descriptions of static posture (e.g., ‘standing’, ‘crouching’, ‘half-squatting’) are always compliant if visually supported — even if the scene implies potential motion — and should not be penalized unless contradicted by clear visual cues of motion. If both answers are static and factually consistent, preference should be determined by other criteria — not by motion/stability. The criterion must never be used to penalize descriptive accuracy, stylistic preference, or factual errors — only to flag contradictions between visual evidence and motion/stability claims. It must not be applied to stylized, symbolic, or artistic representations of action — unless the visual cues clearly depict physical motion (e.g., motion blur, posture). The goal is to ensure that motion or stability descriptions are grounded in visual evidence — not in plausible but unsupported inferences — and to avoid misapplication to static or non-motion questions. Annotators must not use this criterion to resolve ties or evaluate disqualified candidates — and must always defer to visual_grounding and factual_consistency first. If an answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded, it is disqualified from all criteria — regardless of motion/stability relevance — and the criterion is irrelevant. The criterion must be applied only to definitive claims — not speculative, cautious, or non-definitive statements (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘may be’, ‘appears to be’) — which are visually consistent and not penalized. Descriptions like ‘in the process of driving’ are not definitive and are allowed as long as they are plausible and non-contradictory. The criterion must explicitly state that it does not penalize non-definitive, cautious language — only definitive claims that contradict visual evidence — to avoid over-penalizing accurate but cautious inferences. It must also clarify that it does not apply to static positional or depth descriptions (e.g., ‘water reaches knees’) — even if they describe water level — to prevent misapplication. The criterion must explicitly state that it is not a filter for comparing disqualified candidates — and that any answer that violates visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image is disqualified from all criteria — regardless of motion/stability relevance. Finally, the criterion must explicitly warn that it is not applicable to non-motion-related questions — and that workers must report ‘inapplicable’ when motion is not the focus — without attempting to infer or interpret structure or context. Additionally, the criterion must explicitly exclude behavioral, biological, or contextual inferences — even if grounded — as long as they do not involve physical motion or stability. It should clearly state that it only applies to claims about physical motion or stability (e.g., running, leaning, stationary) — not to speculative or cautious behavioral interpretations. The criterion must also explicitly state that it is not applicable to questions about perception, threat response, or biological plausibility — which are evaluated under other criteria. Finally, it must clarify that non-definitive, cautious language (e.g., ‘might be able to perceive’) is acceptable — even if contextually plausible — as long as it does not imply physical motion or instability. The criterion must explicitly prohibit penalizing accurate descriptions of visual phenomena like reflections, shadows, or compositional elements — even if they are not motion/stability claims — and must avoid conflating such descriptions with 'factual errors' or 'hallucinations'. It must also clarify that 'UI design' or 'mirror effect' are valid visual descriptions if grounded in the image, not errors. The criterion should prohibit penalizing accurate, non-motion descriptions under this criterion and must explicitly warn against misinterpreting visual phenomena as factual errors. The criterion must explicitly and unambiguously state that it is only applicable when the question explicitly or implicitly asks about motion, action, or physical stability — and must explicitly require annotators to report 'inapplicable' when the question is about composition, static positioning, or non-motion-related visual elements. The criterion should also explicitly warn against penalizing motion claims in non-motion contexts — even if they are factually consistent — and should clarify that 'drawing an arc' is not a motion claim in a static compositional image unless explicitly implied by visual cues (e.g., motion blur, trajectory lines).

criteria.name: temporal_coherence_of_visual_sequence
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s factual claims about motion, action, or state sequence are consistent with explicit visual cues of temporal progression — defined as motion blur, overlapping frames, sequential posture, dynamic object arrangement, or implied causal order — but ONLY when such cues are present in the image. It is inapplicable to static scenes, abstract compositions, or questions that do not involve implied temporal order (e.g., object identification, color description, spatial arrangement). Annotators must first verify that the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from temporal_coherence evaluation and cannot be compared under this criterion. When applicable, it penalizes only definitive, factual claims that contradict visual temporal evidence (e.g., describing a person as ‘just finished running’ when motion blur indicates ongoing motion) — but does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) or aesthetic, stylistic, or interpretive language — as these are not temporal claims and are evaluated under other criteria. It does NOT penalize minor factual errors, misinterpretations, or omissions — those are handled under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. It is NOT a tiebreaker — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image, specificity) if this criterion is inapplicable or if both answers are factually consistent and temporally coherent. If no visual cues of sequence are present, the criterion is inapplicable — and workers must report ‘inapplicable’ and defer to other criteria — without attempting to evaluate or disqualify answers — even if one contains a factual error. The criterion must be applied strictly to dynamic visual evidence — not inferred motion, contextual plausibility, or implied causality — and must prioritize direct visual cues over speculative or inferential assumptions. If visual evidence contradicts an inferred temporal sequence (e.g., motion blur vs. stationary inference), the visual evidence must be respected — and the answer penalized if it violates it. The criterion must not be used to evaluate factual accuracy, visual grounding, or completeness — only temporal alignment with visual cues. Workers must explicitly flag ‘inapplicable’ when the image is static or the question does not involve temporal order — and must not use this criterion to resolve preference in static scenes, factually inconsistent answers, or when it is inapplicable.
